title: The development and optimization of an innovative piezoelectric energy harvester on the basis of vapor-induced vibrations

sections.heading: The development and optimization of an innovative piezoelectric energy harvester on the basis of vapor-induced vibrations

sections.heading: a b s t r a c t
sections.text:
Various energy harvesters were developed by several energy sources. In the heat pipe, the vapor momentum can be used to drive a mechanical structure to generate electricity. To bridge this gap, this study experimentally designed an energy harvester on the basis of a vapor-induced vibration for the innovative heat pipe application. The energy harvester, comprising a cantilever beam and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), was designed using finite element method and the genetic algorithm (GA) to reach the resonance point. Copper, aluminum, and polyethylene (PE) were used as the material of the cantilever beam for the energy harvester. The optimized energy harvester was examined using a shocker, and obtained the output voltage. The output power of the harvester was affected by the vapor velocity, cantilever beam material, and natural frequency. The output voltages of the PVDF with the cantilever beam are better than the one of PVDF without the cantilever beam and it increased $3 6 7 \%$ , $3 9 3 \%$ , and $4 7 0 \%$ ascantilever beam is copper, aluminum, and polyethylene, respectively. The theoretical and practical implication, limitations of the present study for future studies are presented and studied.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
To harvest energy from an exist and past-useless energy has attracted a great deal of attention in recent years. It can practice the self-powered sensor and replace the battery. Various energy harvesters were developed by several energy sources such as electromagnetic mechanism [1], radio frequency (RF) [2], piezoelectric film [3] et ale. These phenomena have recently motivated scholars to conduct the various type of harvesting. A review paper exhibits the relation between piezoelectric device and fluid flow [4]. A kind of heat pipe energy harvester based on the magnetic/vibrating mechanism has been proposed based on the fluid flow [5]. The spring-type piezoelectric transducer, lead zirconate titanate (PZT), combined with heat pipe has been applied on energy harvester [6].

Heat pipe is a simple device that can rapidly transfer heat, and it is divided into three sections: an evaporator section, adiabatic section, and condenser section. When the heat pipe is heated, the working fluid boils and vaporizes. The vapor travels along the vapor spacing to the condenser section, and the condensate working fluid is returned to the evaporator section by gravity or capillary structure. The process of removing heat involves the working fluid vapor flowing from the evaporator to the condenser. A pressure difference is created between the condenser and the evaporator. The vapor momentum can be used to drive a mechanical structure to generate electricity. An energy harvesting device is proposed by Hsu and Leo [7,8] first. A turbine driven by the low pressure solar boiler enabled the power generation. Pryputniewicz and Haapala [9] proposed a concept that involves a turbine is used in a heat pipe. On the basis of this concept, Akbarzadeh et al. [10] developed a thermosyphon Rankine (TSR) engine for harvesting geothermal and solar energy. The TSR engine could harvest $3 \mathrm { k W }$ of power as the temperature difference between the evaporator and condenser sections was $3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C$ approximately and the input power was $1 0 0 \mathrm { k W } ,$ , thus increasing the thermoelectric conversion efficiency by $3 \%$ approximately.

The static friction of turbine has to overcome before driving it. Static friction is relatively high in small-scale turbine systems, and results in the low efficiency. To reduce the friction of a small-scale generator, the turbine can be replaced by piezoelectric material to generate electric power through the vapor momentum in the heat pipe.

In general, piezoelectric material is used to harvest environmental energy with a wireless sensor served as the power source. However, the output power is still insufficient, therefore, increasing the output power or conversion efficiency is still the focus of many studies. Li et al. [11] investigated the output voltages of AlN doped $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } } }$ piezoelectric film connected in series and in parallel, with a low vibrating frequency affected by a touch response. The material properties are studied for enhancing the voltage response [12]. Singh et al. [13] proposed a method for increasing the bistable distance of cantilever beam of piezoelectric energy harvester. To increase the efficiency, the shape of piezoelectric module is discussed based on the enhancing vibration [14]. Shin et al. [15] proposed an innovative application about piezoelectric power generator on roadway energy harvesting. A spherical proof mass is proposed for resulting in the vibration of cantilever-based energy harvester [16]. This design is to vibrate the cantilever beam easier than the traditional single beam.

Kong et al. proposed the energy harvester induced by water flow. The vortices create unsteady loading and induce vibrations with a predictable frequency and amplitude [17].Pressure drop and vertices induced by fluid flow occur in numerous engineering designs such as bridges, stacks, transmission lines, aircraft control surfaces, offshore structures, thermowells, engines, and heat exchangers [18]. Fujarra et al. [19] investigated the flow-induced vibrations of a flexible cantilever, determining that the transverse amplitude response of the cantilever increased with the flow velocity in the initial branch. In the lower branch, the amplitude decreased as the velocity increased. Because the natural frequency of the cantilever was higher in the streamwise direction, streamwise oscillations were excited at higher speeds. Doaré and Michelin [20] investigated the energy harvested from the vibration of a plate in an axial flow, and they developed the equations for fully coupled linear dynamics of fluid-solid and electrical systems. He and Gao [21] proposed the harvesting wind energy on the basis of flow-induced vibrations. The experimental results showed that the critical wind speed was in the range of 3.2 and $3 . 4 \mathrm { m } /$ s. When the wind speed was $3 . 2 \ : \mathrm { m } / s$ , which is lower than the critical speed, nearly no vibration of the cantilever was observed, and the root mean square (RMS) open-circuit voltage was approximately $1 \textrm { m V }$ . Hu et al. [22] experimentally examined the performance of a circular cylinder-based piezoelectric wind energy harvester associated with two rods attached on two sides of the main circular cylinder at the circumferential locations of $4 5 ^ { \circ }$ and $6 0 ^ { \circ }$ . They found that the performance of a circular cylinder-based wind energy harvester could be enhanced by two triangular rods at the circumferential location of $6 0 ^ { \circ }$ . Shan et al. [23] presented a new underwater double piezoelectric energy harvester (DPEH) system. They indicated that the output power of DPEH was higher than that of the single piezoelectric energy harvester system. Nasser et al. [24] investigated the effects of the spacing distance between two magnets on the buckling configuration of the energy harvester. The numerical results displayed that the variation of the spacing distance produces a variation of the natural frequency, which represented the spacing distance and load resistance can be adjusted for efficient and broadband energy harvesting from flow-induced vibration.

In comparison to the previous literatures, the optimization and performance of the energy harvester based on heat pipes has not been well-studied. This gap is addressed by the present study, which utilizes the integration of experiment and optimization to obtain the optimal performance of piezoelectric transducer within the heat pipe. Our team [25] proposes an innovated micro heat pipe harvester based on the micro-piezoelectric vibration-induced power device. The bending of the piezoelectric material by vapor impacting results in the vapor momentum converts to the power. The current study also addresses three main limitations in the prior literature on experimental practice, optimization and materials. To address these limitations, the current study utilizes the genetic algorithm, experimental validation to obtain the best performance of the piezoelectric transducer and compares the efficiency based on the different subtract.

The aforementioned information can be used to investigate the vibrations induced by a uniform fluid flow in a flexible circular cylinder. The application of the fluid-structure interaction can induce vibrations in a flexible structure and cause vortex shedding. Converting thermal energy into power is achieved by these vibrations. In this study, a suitable cantilever beam combined with piezoelectric material is investigated to reach a resonance point by using multiphysics COMSOL [26] and GA optimization method. To verify the optimal geometry of the cantilever beam, harvesters are examined using a shocker. Finally, the harvesters are driven by steam for investigating the feasibility of using a microgenerator in a heat pipe. A vapor generator is used to evaluate the performance of PVDF combined with the cantilever beam.

sections.heading: 2. Experimental apparatus and procedure
sections.text:
The experimental system of vapor generator includes a heater, a data logger, the power supply, working fluid tank, and holder. Fig. 1 shows a schematic representation of the experimental system [25]. In this study, the working fluid was water, and it was heated to be the vapor to drive the piezoelectric energy harvester. The heater power is adjusted by voltage or current. As the heated power is applied, the water vaporized at boiling temperature. Fig. 2 illustrates the dimensions and photograph of the vapor generator module. There is a small hole (diameter is $1 . 0 \mathrm { m m }$ ) on the top of tank served as a nozzle to enable the vapor to exit. In this study, PVDF is used as the vibrating sample to generate electricity. For enhancing the bending of PVDF, a cantilever beam is affixed to it. Three kinds of materials of cantilever beam, namely aluminum, copper, and polyethylene (PE), are used, and their mechanical properties are listed in Table 1. Fig. 3 shows the initial dimensions of PVDF and the cantilever beam. ![](images/2a58ce0bad2efcf14a1bb60590b4a05faa940b90a0ec5d5ab7f8e7fb7c090353.jpg) Fig. 1. The schematic diagram of the experimental system [25]. In this study, the cantilever beam is divided into three sections (Fig. 3(b)): the vapor-impacted section, PVDF-adhered section, and fixed section. The vapor-impacted section is placed on the exit of the vapor generator nozzle. The spacing distance (H) between the vapor-impacted section and the nozzle exit could be adjusted from 2 to $1 0 \mathrm { m m }$ . Electricity is generated for the reason of the bending of the PVDF-adhered section. The temperatures of the heater and tank are measured by using four thermocouples and logged using the data logger. The output voltage, current, and frequency of energy harvesting are recorded using a GWINSTEK GDS-2062 and KEITHLEY Model 237 Source Measure Unit. The uncertainties in the output voltage and current were $\pm ( 4 \% \times | \mathrm { R e a d o u t } | + 0 . 8 \mathrm { m V } )$ and $\pm ( 0 . 0 5 \% + 2 0 0 \mathrm { p A } )$ , respectively. To investigate the kinetic energy related to the PVDF harvester, the vapor velocity is measured using a hot wire with an uncertainty of $\pm 0 . 0 2 5 \mathrm { m } / s$ . ![](images/a86bd604cc1db926afcb22007853d43df00c28a3993d9a78ceb24497bfd75b99.jpg) Fig. 2. Resonance vibration can amplify relative bending displacement considerably. Therefore, microgenerators, which can mechanically resonate at the frequency of a vapor-induced vibration, will generate maximum electrical power. The fundamental natural frequency of the cantilever can be approximated as follows: $$ f _ { n } = { \sqrt { \frac { k } { m } } } $$ Eq. (1) indicates that the natural frequency of the cantilever energy harvester depends on the variations of the geometry of the cantilever beam. In this study, the dimension of the cantilever beam within the vapor-impacted section was optimized using the GA. Typically, gradient methods can be used to solve optimization problems. However, a gradient-based method is problematic in the presence of a local extreme value. This problem can be avoided as the GA is used. The numerical design approach is developed by combining a direct problem solver, COMSOL code based on the finite element model, with an optimal method (genetic algorithm, GA). The COMSOL package is used as the subroutine to solve the vibration of cantilever beam associated with the variation of the length of the cantilever beam during the iterative optimal process. The GA optimizer and commercial COMSOL code with a script program are connected through the interface program of MATLAB software to compute the natural frequency of the cantilever beam of the harvester. The GA is a powerful optimization technique that is based on natural selection, mimicking the concept of survival of the fittest. Here, the GA entailed using individual encoding and decoding, operators (mutation and crossover), a fitness criterion, and an elitism selection function (selection) to process the optimization. The optimization procedure is described briefly as follows: Step 1. Generate a random population. Step 2. Evaluate each individual assigning a fitness value according to an objective function. Step 3. Use selection and elitism to form the mating pool. Step 4. Apply crossover and mutation. Step 5. If generation of process approaches the convergence, then the optimization process will end. If not, the process will repeat steps 2, 3, and 4 until a termination criterion is met or a fixed number of generations have been completed. The generation number, population, crossover probability, and mutation probability of this optimization are 30, 100, 0.6, and 0.01, respectively.

sections.heading: 3. Experimental results and discussion
sections.text:
Through the vaporization of working fluid, the fluid-structure interaction can result in the vibrations of a flexible structure of PVDF to produce the output power. To derive the objective function of the optimization process, the frequency of the vapor-induced vibration engendered by the fluid-structure interaction is measured at various velocities (Fig. 4 and Table 2). The results indicate that the output power is demonstrated to exhibit a sine wave function, and that the frequency of the vapor-induced vibration is $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ approximately and unaffected by the velocity of the nozzle exit. In this study, for inducing a resonance of the cantilever beam and vortex shedding, the objective function of the optimization method is assumed that the vibrated frequency of cantilever beam approaches $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Fig. 5 illustrates the effects of the spacing distance (H) between the nozzle exit and the harvester on vapor velocity and the peak output power of the harvester as the input power is 100 W (velocity of nozzle exit is $3 . 8 \mathrm { m } / s \cdot$ ). The vapor velocity is a function of the H of the harvester from the nozzle exit. According to the results, the vapor centerline velocity clearly decreases at $\mathrm { H } \geq 4 \ : \mathrm { m m }$ because of the effect of the jet potential core length. As the vapor centerline velocity decreases, the diffusion of turbulence levels increased at $\mathrm { H } \geq 4 \mathrm { m m }$ . The peak voltage is only slightly affected by spacing distance at $\mathrm { H } \le 6 \ : \mathrm { m m }$ . However, at $\mathrm { H } > 6 \mathrm { m m }$ , the peak voltage is equal to zero because of the velocity diminishing and jet spreading. Therefore, the spacing distance between the nozzle exit and the impacted section of the thermal energy harvester is preset at $5 \mathrm { m m }$ for the entire experiment. The initial natural frequencies of PVDF and PVDF combined with the cantilever beam are evaluated using Multiphysics COMSOL software (Table 3). The simulated results indicated that the initial natural frequency of the cantilever beam of the energy harvester depended on the cantilever material. The initial natural frequencies of PVDF, PVDF with copper, aluminum, and the PE cantilever beam are 142.13, 36.25, 54.25, and $8 . 2 5 \mathrm { H z }$ , respectively. The GA was used to optimize the length of the cantilever beam such that the beam bending displacement could be amplified at the resonance point. The objective function of the vapor-induced vibration in the optimization method was $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Fig. 6 and Table 3 show the optimized lengths of the cantilever beam. The simulated results reveal the optimal lengths of PVDF with copper, aluminum and PE cantilever beam at $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ frequency for the vapor-induced vibration are 52.45, 57.77 and $3 8 . 8 5 \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. To clearly understand the effects of resonance, the optimized energy harvester is examined using a shocker at various excited frequencies (Fig. 7). In Fig. 7, the vertical axis indicates the dimensionless open-circuit voltage of the energy harvester. The experimental results reveal that the open-circuit voltage peaks at an excited frequency of $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . The peak of open-circuit voltage decreases substantially as the excited frequency deviated from the resonance point. However, the available bandwidth is nonsignificant affected by the cantilever beam material. The optimal lengths of the copper, aluminum, and PE cantilever beams are 53.72, 58.44, and $3 7 . 3 \mathrm { m m }$ (Table 3), respectively. Comparing the optimized lengths of the copper, aluminum, and PE cantilever beams between the experiment and simulation reveals the error of $2 . 4 \%$ , $1 . 2 \%$ , and $4 . 0 \%$ , respectively. sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In this study, the feasibility of combining PVDF with various cantilever beam materials, according to vapor-flow-induced vortex shedding, is investigated using an experiment and optimization method. A cantilever beam with suitable dimensions is designed using the optimization method and Multiphysics COMSOL software to approach the resonance point and amplify the output voltage. The primary results can be summarized as follows:

(1) The harvester output power is only slightly affected by the spacing distance at $\mathrm { H } \le 6 \ : \mathrm { m m }$ . However, at $\mathrm { H } > 6 \mathrm { m m }$ , the output power is equal to zero because of the velocity diminishing and jet spreading. The vapor velocity is a function of the spacing distance of the harvester from the nozzle exit. According to the results, the vapor centerline velocity clearly decreases at $\mathrm { H } \geq 4 \ : \mathrm { m m }$ because of the effect of the jet potential core length.   
(2) The vapor flows over the cantilever beam which results in the $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ of periodicity vibration. The frequency of the vapor-induced vibration is not affected by the cantilever beam material or vapor velocity. However, the output power is related to the vibration amplitude of the cantilever beam of the energy harvester, which depends on the resonance, cantilever beam material, and vapor velocity. The output power of the PE cantilever peaks at a high vapor velocity as the frequency of the cantilever beam vibration approaches the resonance point.   
(3) The simulation built by COMSOL is verified by the experiment. Then, the GA is used to optimize the dimensions of the cantilever beam for achieving an objective function of $6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Comparing the optimized lengths of the copper, aluminum, and PE cantilever beams between the experiment and simulation revealed errors of $2 . 4 \%$ , $1 . 2 \%$ , and $4 . 0 \%$ , respectively.   
(4) The RMS output power is slightly affected by the cantilever beam materials at vapor velocities lower than $2 . 6 \ : \mathrm { m } / s$ . However, the output power for the PE material increases sharply for velocities greater than $3 . 2 \ : \mathrm { m } / s$ .

This study investigates and optimizes the performance of an energy harvester on the basis of vapor-induced vibration. The thermoelectric conversion performance for the energy harvester is significantly affected by experimental parameters. The results can serve as reference data for using heat pipe generators in waste heat recovery.
